11535-views-a-foot-or-europe-seen-with-k:
J. Bayard Taylor's Views A-Foot was entered in 1846, with a preface by N. P. Willis. Willis praises a printer's apprentice turned traveller and author, whose talent he had spotted early. The book tells of Europe seen with knapsack and staff.

Part one moves from the voyage to a day in Ireland. Ben Lomond and the Highland lakes follow. Then the tour crosses the Continent, with frescoed halls at Munich recalling Charlemagne, Barbarossa, and Rudolph of Hapsburg. The book is a young American's walking tour, written with energy and a poet's eye.
15300-mike-flannery-on-duty-and-off:
Ellis Parker Butler's 1909 humor book follows Mike Flannery, an express office man at Westcote, on duty and off. Three stories, Just Like a Cat, The Three Hundred, and Fleas Will Be Fleas, make the set, with pictures by Gustavus Widney. A frontispiece jokes over the name Phoenix.

Flannery watches a land company rip the top off Seiler's Hill and dump it into a swampy meadow, soon to burst into streets and houses. Cats, helpers, and office talk supply the comedy. Readers who like Irish-American humor will find Mike warm, funny, and full of small-town bustle.
15971-polly-of-the-hospital-staff:
A children's hospital story by Emma C. Dowd, issued by Houghton Mifflin in Boston and New York in 1912, printed at the Riverside Press, Cambridge. Dowd dedicates the book to the Mother of Polly. Polly, a girl on the hospital staff, brings cheer to wards and nurses alike. Dowd writes with warmth for sick children and their helpers.

The cherry-pudding story and the election of Polly open the book, with Popover, David, and Lone Star's assistance. Elsie's birthday, the little sad lady, and a warning from Aunt Jane follow, with a night of song and the ward's anniversary. Polly plays Eva to close. The book delights as a hospital tale: a girl who heals by kindness, in a place of pain.
16197-one-third-off:
Irvin S. Cobb's 1921 Doran volume, illustrated by Tony Sarg, gathers humorous pieces with a telling frontispiece: the author weighing himself and crediting the scales with a profound shock. He dedicates the book to Harry M. Stevens, who in times gone by helped him put that one third on. Contents range from a plea for Old Cap Collier and the abandoned farmers to the life of the party, eating in two or three languages, and Europe revised.

Roughing it de luxe, Cobb's anatomy, and the thunders of silence show his range, from dieting and travel to small-town life and war talk. Cobb, famed for Old Judge Priest, writes warm, drawling American humor. Readers who like newspaper wit at its most companionable will enjoy this cheerful miscellany.
22879-paul-patoff:
F. Marion Crawford places Paul Patoff in the East in his 1887 novel. Even the horses feel the weather in the excerpt. Haroun al Raschid, a gray, shakes raindrops restlessly from his mane, longing, it seems, for hot sand and desert sun. The wind, another rider notes, is the wind of home.

Crawford knew Constantinople and Rome well, and he builds the tale on diplomatic and social ground between East and West. Paul Patoff, a Russian diplomat's son, moves through intrigue where manners and danger intertwine. Crawford's novels were international bestsellers, prized for polished scenes and cosmopolitan settings. This one offers melodrama with a traveler's eye, written by a man who had lived inside the world he describes.
23373-the-eagle-cliff:
R. M. Ballantyne opened this tale with a young man on a penny farthing cycling toward London, who knocks down an elderly lady and flees at the sight of a policeman. A telegram soon calls him to join friends on a yacht bound for the islands off the north west of Britain, and he goes.

Fog wrecks the yacht, but the party gets ashore near a large house, where a gentleman and his family take them in as guests. Fishing, shooting, bird watching, sailing, and a charming young lady fill the days that follow, with the Eagle Cliff itself looming over the fun. Ballantyne writes the isles with fresh, lasting images, making this one of his most fondly recalled books for young readers.
28646-solar-stiff:
Chas. A. Stopher's Solar Stiff opens with Probos Five of Mercury losing altitude over a white expanse. His Interstar Runabout's fuel system fails, and five pairs of eyes cannot find a landing place. Five pairs of arms work controls in vain, and the Mercurian philosopher accepts death, since Planet Three's frigid climate kills his kind and no smashed cruiser returns.

Probos Five stretches his twenty-foot trunk, four heads watching the compass points while a fifth watches the panel. He thinks of his wife Lingua Four, fourteen feet tall and growing a rare fifth head, and of his son Probos Two. The blazing white polar region rushes up, promising a quick end. Readers get a comic alien crash tale, told from the falling pilot's five minds.
31214-broad-sword-and-single-stick-with-:
R. G. Allanson-Winn and C. Phillipps-Wolley's manual, published by G. Bell and Sons in the All-England Series, teaches the fighting arts of the late Victorian gentleman. Chapters take up the quarter-staff, the broad-sword, single-stick, and the bayonet, with further chapters on the cudgel, shillalah, walking-stick, umbrella, and other weapons of self-defense.

Illustrated and priced for the popular series that also covered cricket, tennis, golf, rowing, and boxing, the book gives stances, guards, cuts, and practice. It serves readers who might need a stick more than a sword. It remains a lively record of how Edwardian England taught its sons to handle themselves.
42111-and-then-the-town-took-off:
And Then the Town Took Off is a science fiction novel by Richard Wilson, published by Ace Books in 1960. Its premise is announced in the cover copy's headline: the town of Superior, Ohio, has run off the map.

One night Superior simply picks itself up and rises two miles above the earth, leaving a vast pit where it stood. Radio messages say the town has seceded, and its calm citizens credit a local crackpot professor with the feat. The professor, however, has no idea how to bring them down. Don Cort, stranded aboard the floating town, must find a way to anchor it or spend his life on the smallest and nuttiest planet in the galaxy. The opening chapter begins with a truck driver who nearly drives into the pit on Route 202.
43419-jiglets-a-series-of-sidesplitting-:
Jiglets is a joke book by Walter Jones in the Street and Smith Humor Library. Street and Smith of New York held the rights in the year 1903. The book sold for twenty-five cents as number three of its line. Its subtitle calls the jokes sidesplitting gyrations reeled off for laughs. Jones warns the reader up front about the book's many pictures.

The pictures are pure ornament, not keys to the jokes, he insists. Any one joke, if you like it, is worth eleven times the price. He signs that note in a confidential tone to the dear reader. The patter opens on a stage with eleven folk in the house. Jones thanks the man with hair in the front row of seats. Tales of touring New England with a Shakespeare company follow on. Hamlet won him eggs in the eye, saved up for an omelet.
44570-the-sunshade-the-glove-the-muff:
Sunshade, the Glove, the Muff, by Octave Uzanne, treats dress accessories in depth. Paul Avril drew the pictures for the London edition of eighteen eighty three. Nimmo and Bain of the Strand issued the English volume that year. The first part covers the sunshade, the parasol, and the umbrella together.

Uzanne opens that no one can fix when the parasol was first devised. Its origin hides in the night of time, the text concedes at once. A Bible phrase on shelter from the sun hints an eastern birth. Nineveh carvings and Thebes tomb art show parasols in remote ages past. China used the parasol two thousand years before Christ, Uzanne reports.
44900-the-life-of-sir-john-falstaff:
The Life of Sir John Falstaff, published at London in 1858, is Robert Brough's mock biography of Shakespeare's fat knight. George Cruikshank drew the pictures, and the work came out monthly in ten parts, two plates in each. Brough dedicated the book to his sister Mary, whose care had helped him finish it through hard times.

The preface argues that Falstaff feels more real than most figures of true history. He walks through events that happened, beside men who lived. Brough treats that illusion with respect, giving the knight a full life from authentic sources. Dates and local color are kept straight, so the joke never breaks its own spell.
51574-the-stuff:
Henry Slesar wrote this tale of a dying man and a disputed drug. The story ran in Galaxy Magazine in August 1961. Paula Hills begs Doctor Bernstein for no more lies at the start. Her husband Andy has lain in coma for four days.

Bernstein calls the drug Senopoline curious and little known to him. Only Paula, as wife, can permit its use on Andy. She has lived with lies for a year, she tells him. A sheeted, still mound on a hospital bed frames the choice. Ritter drew the pictures for the magazine printing of the tale as issued here.
61121-the-lay-of-the-sheriff:
The Lay of the Sheriff is a comic verse play by Philip Lybbe Powys Lybbe of Hardwick, printed in London in 1869 for private circulation. The piece celebrates, in mock-heroic couplets, the author's son Henry's year as High Sheriff of Oxfordshire in 1843. A Latin dedication addresses the Reverend Edward Moore, rector of Whitchurch, and the prologue is spoken by the sheriff's mother.

Mrs Vanderstegen's prologue is a long, delighted monologue. She can hardly believe her good fortune, pointing to her full cupboards, her old chair, her brocaded dresses and her slow carriage as proof that she truly is the sheriff's mother. She orders the household to feast on mutton bones, bread and small beer, and to sing the sheriff's praise. The humour is domestic and affectionate: county ceremony seen from the kitchen, with the proud mother stealing every scene she is in.
62063-the-girls-of-greycliff:
Harriet Pyne Grove wrote a school story for Burt of New York, copyrighted in 1923. It is one of a set of Greycliff tales for girls. The big halls are full again of laughter and talk. Trunks bump up the inclines fixed at the stairs, and one small girl slides down an incline on a newspaper.

Lilian comes flying down the wide steps to meet Hilary at the gate. The two hug, part, and hug again in the hall. Hilary has missed some letters by not going home first. Cathalina, she learns, is truly coming back. The friends are all to be together in a suite in Greycliff Hall. The book opens in high spirits, with a full school year ahead.
62079-cathalina-at-greycliff:
Harriet Pyne Grove wrote this girls' tale, printed by the A L Burt Company of New York with a 1923 copyright. It stands in her Greycliff Girls series, with The Girls of Greycliff, the girls in camp, Greycliff Heroines, and Greycliff Wings. A plate shows Cathalina turning a boat shoreward while Lilian strums a guitar. Cathalina Van Buskirk, fourteen, has her hair done up high against the heat.

She hopes her mother will soon choose the mountains. Her brother Phil is coming home for good, and his needs will settle the summer's plan. Her room, in blue, white, and silver, was chosen by Cathalina herself when the new home was finished. Grove writes the school and summer life of a well-off girl and her friends.
6564-the-love-tiff:
Molière joins two pieces in this five-act comedy from 1656, first played at Béziers while the States General of Languedoc met there. The longer part borrows its plot from an Italian comedy, turning on a child swapped at birth, a trick that runs through many old plays and tales. The shorter, finer part is Molière's own, and it is the part the French stage still plays.

Lovers quarrel, servants scheme, and mistaken kinship keeps the plot in a spin until the truth unties it. The verse moves fast, and the jokes land through talk rather than through stage tricks. For readers new to Molière, The Love-Tiff shows both his debts to older comedy and his own fresh voice.
65938-the-cosmic-bluff:
The Cosmic Bluff is a science fiction story by Mack Reynolds. The tale appeared in a magazine of science and fantasy in October 1952. A blurb tells how Earth's champion challenged invaders to a duel in an arena. The bluff was grand, but the invaders called it with a champion of their own.

The narrator, Jak, tells the story in his own slangy voice. To the whole Solar System he is a big shot, he admits. Only two people know he is a fake: Suzi, and Jak himself. Suzi stands in his vast new penthouse atop a two hundred story building. She calls him phony, humbug, and four flusher in turn. Portraits, statues, and ghost written books fill the room as proof of his swollen fame. The tale turns on how such a fraud came to stand for Earth.
74444-the-philosophy-of-jake-haiden-late:
Philosophy of Jake Haiden gathers newspaper columns by Jacob K Huff, of Reading, Pennsylvania. Huff wrote under names such as Jake Haiden and Faraway Moses. The pieces were selected from the columns of the Reading Times. A biographical appreciation by his friend Henry W Shoemaker, president of that paper, opens the book. The Reading edition is dated nineteen eleven. A portrait of Huff stands at its front.

Sudden death in the midst of work throws a career into bolder relief, the appreciation begins. Huff struggled long against obscurity before fame greeted him, it says. His message spoke against class distinctions and a self made aristocracy, the sketch holds. Yet he viewed the big world from the porch of a modest cottage, it notes. His hamlet had no railroad, no trolley, and few strangers ever found it.
76570-woodcliff:
Harriet B McKeever wrote a novel published at Philadelphia in 1865, entered for copyright the year before. McKeever had written Edith's Ministry, Sunshine, and Flounced Robe. Chapter one is the sea shore. A ride on horseback and Maddy's triumph follow. Too proud to bend names the fourth chapter. Youthful visions and a Scotch matron continue.

The cottage and the hall oppose two households. Boston relatives visit, and home again follows. Sunshine at the hall and shadows at the cottage state the contrast plainly. A mother's life sorrow deepens the middle. Lindsay and Blakiston published many such domestic tales for Sunday school and family reading.
77391-the-story-of-puff:
Livingston wrote this child tale told by Puff, a pet canary bird. Lothrop printed the book in Boston in 1883. Puff says the canary family is a good old family indeed. A girl named Rita first takes him from mother and kin.

Rita wears a blue dress and white sunbonnet in that first scene. Puff screams in fear as she shuts him in a dark basket. Plates show Dody, Rita, cherry breakfasts, and a lovely new nest. The tale follows a small bird life through love, loss, and sweet song. The Lothrop house issued the tale at Boston.
78247-plays-by-leonid-andreyeff:
Scribner of New York issued three plays by the Russian writer Leonid Andreyeff in an authorized edition. The rights date from 1915, and this printing came in 1923. Meader and Scott turned the plays into English, and a life of the author stands at the front.

Andreyeff was born on August 9, 1871, at Orel, some two hundred miles south of Moscow. His father died while he was still at school, and want dogged him through his law studies. Three times despair drove him to try to take his own life. He painted portraits to live, then turned to newspaper work. Gorki marked his early tales and helped him on. Fame came in 1901 with a book of stories. The plays in this volume are The Black Maskers, The Life of Man, and The Sabine Women.
79562-switch-off:
Switch Off, or The War of the Students, is a boys' tale by Oliver Optic. It is the fourth book of the Lake Shore Series. The first three are Through by Daylight, Lightning Express, and On Time. Brake Up and Bear and Forbear close the set of six. The book came out in Boston from Lee and Shepard, with a copyright date of 1897 as the pack states.

The title page lists the long row of Optic's other works. Among them are the Army and Navy Stories, the Great Western Series, and the Boat-Club and Starry-Flag sets. Young America Abroad and the Yacht-Club Series stand in the list as well. The tale at hand is a school story of rival students, told in the manner of his many series for boys.
britannica-1911-banff:
Banff is a royal burgh, seaport, and capital of Banffshire in Scotland. It stands on high ground on the left bank of the Deveron at its mouth, fifty miles north-west of Aberdeen by rail. Its population in 1901 was 7,161. Malcolm IV granted its first charter in 1163, and later kings added privileges.

Scarcely a trace remains of the old castle where Archbishop Sharp was born; the modern Banff Castle of the earl of Seafield stands on its site. The 1911 Britannica entry lists the county buildings, a town hall with a spire 100 feet high, Chalmers hospital, and an academy in the Grecian style. Its museum holds works of James Ferguson, the astronomer, a son of the district's mechanical genius.
britannica-1911-cardiff:
Cardiff is a city and seaport of South Wales. It is the county town of Glamorganshire. It stands on the river Taff, near its outflow. It lies some 145 miles from London by rail. This long 1911 Britannica article surveys the city. Cardiff is the terminus of the Taff Vale railway. The Rhymney railway also ends at its docks. The Glamorganshire canal, opened in 1794, links it to Merthyr Tydfil.

The article stresses the city's phenomenal growth. In 1801 Cardiff held only 1870 inhabitants. By 1831 the figure had risen to 6187. Coal traffic built the great docks that followed. The Cardiff Railway Company owns all the docks. The article describes the docks, streets and public buildings. It covers the coal trade and the city's government. It also gives Cardiff's history from Roman times onward.
britannica-1911-crieff:
Crieff, a burgh town in Perthshire, Scotland, is described in a 1911 Britannica article. It is the capital of Strathearn, near eighteen miles west of Perth by rail. Its count in 1901 was 5,208 people. The town sits on the south slopes of a hill on the left bank of the Earn.

Crieff is built in the main as one street with side streets at right angles. Its air is called the most healthy in mid Scotland, pure and dry. Its charter is said to date from 1218, and it hosted the courts of the earls of Strathearn till 1747. A great cattle fair once famed there moved to Falkirk in 1770. Trades list cloth of cotton, linen, and wool, plus leather.
britannica-1911-frisches-haff: Frisches Haff is a lagoon on the Baltic coast of Germany, in East and West Prussia between Danzig and Königsberg. It runs 52 miles long and from 4 to 12 miles broad, with an area of 332 square miles. A narrow spit of land cuts it off from the Baltic Sea. A storm tore that barrier open in 1510, and the channel then formed, now dredged to 22 feet, gives ships a passage. Five rivers flow into it, and the Frisching probably gave it its name.
britannica-1911-macduff:
Macduff is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a seaport town in Scotland. The town lies in Banffshire, on the mouth of the Deveron. It stands one mile east of Banff. A count from 1901 gives the town 3431 people. The site was first a fishing village called Doune. The earl of Fife bought the place in the early 1700s.

The second earl gave the town its new name, Macduff. He won it a royal charter as a burgh in 1783. He rebuilt the market cross to mark that year. The harbour is safer than the one at Banff. The duke of Fife built it and gave it to the burgh in 1898. Most townsfolk work in the herring trade. Boat building, rope work, and saw mills give other work.
britannica-1911-pastoral-staff:
Pastoral staff is a sign of office in the Christian Church, treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is some five feet long and ends at the top in a crook bent inwards. It is made of metal, ivory, or wood. A metal staff is hollow, and a wood one is most often clad in metal.

The crook is rich with ornament and is parted from the shaft by a boss. The shaft is built in sections held by rings, so it can be taken apart. The staff is the proper sign of cardinals and of bishops. Cardinals may use it only in the churches of their titles, and bishops only in their own dioceses. The pope did not carry one, so far as the record shows from the time of Innocent the Third. Abbots may carry one only by leave of the pope.
britannica-1911-roscoff:
Roscoff is a seaside town and watering place of north-west France, in the department of Finistère, as this 1911 Britannica article describes it. It stands on the English Channel, north-north-west of Morlaix by rail. The town had 1,984 people in 1906, and the commune 5,054, and a narrow channel splits it from the Ile de Batz.

Its tidal port serves fishing and coasting vessels. Many of its people grow early vegetables, for which the mild climate and fertile soil are well suited. The church, from the 1500s, has a fine tower in the style of the revival of learning and holds noteworthy alabaster carvings. A ruined chapel marks the landing of Mary Stuart in 1548, before her betrothal to the dauphin. Charles Edward, the young Pretender, also landed here in 1746 after his defeat at Culloden.
britannica-1911-set-off:
Set-off is, in law, a defence set by statute to the whole or part of a claim made in court. The 1911 Britannica article says it had no place in the old common law. It was made by an act of 1729 for the relief of debtors who could not pay. Such a plea could be used for fixed debts on both sides alone. It did not reach claims for damages, nor claims in equity. By court rules a man sued may set off any claim of his own as a counter claim.

That plea then works like a claim in a cross suit of his own. In building, a set-off is the flat ledge shown where a wall grows thinner. The thick part juts out before the thin part at that line. On plinths the ledge is most times just sloped.
britannica-1911-staff:
Staff is a word and military article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica that follows one short word through many senses. From the Old English staef comes the long stick or pole. It served as a walking aid, as a weapon in the quarter staff, and as a badge of office in the pastoral staff. The word also names the pole that carries a flag and, by way of its old sense of letters, the lines of verse and the ruled lines of music.

The bulk of the article treats the military staff, the body of helpers around a general. That ordered system, it argues, is a modern growth. Later a quartermaster general and his men chose camps, scouted the country, and gathered news, as Cadogan served Marlborough in all three roles at once.
britannica-1911-traill-henry-duff:
Henry Duff Traill, who lived from 1842 to 1900, was a British author and journalist. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica calls him a man of letters first. He was born at Blackheath in August 1842. His father was a magistrate from an old Caithness family.

Traill won a scholarship to Oxford and read natural science there. He then turned to law and was called to the bar in 1869. A schools office post left him time to write at ease. From 1873 he wrote for leading London papers for decades. Weekly verses on the news of the hour made his wit known. A sly pamphlet told the Exodus tale as newspaper parody. That unsigned hit proved him a born humorist at once. In 1897 he became first editor of a new Times weekly.
britannica-1911-tuff:
Tuff is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a rock made of volcanic ashes. The Italian word tufo gives it its name. Tuff consists of the ejecta of craters in eruption. The products of an eruption fall into three groups. Those are steam and other gases, lavas, and ashes. The ashes have not been burnt in any way. They merely resemble cinders in their appearance. They are porous, slaggy pieces of lava in truth.

They became full of bubbles while still plastic. Loose beds of ash cover the slopes of many volcanoes. Three classes of material are found in those beds. True ashes of the kind described form the first class. Lumps of old lavas and tuffs form the second. Those were torn from the crater walls by steam blasts. Pieces of sedimentary rocks form the third class.
britannica-1911-turriff:
Turriff, a burgh of Aberdeenshire in Scotland, is given a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It held 2,273 people in 1901 and lies near the Deveron, north west of Aberdeen by railway through Inveramsay. In the choir of its ancient church, now in ruins, there is a fresco painting of Saint Ninian. 

On the fourteenth of May 1639 the national struggle for civil and religious liberty was opened in the county with the skirmish known as the Trot of Turriff. A few miles south stand the remains of the castle of Towie Barclay, the seat of the old family of the Barclays.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baroness-von-:
Baroness von Droste-Hülshoff was a poet, born at Schloss Hülshoff near Münster in 1797, who died in 1848. After her father's death in 1826, she lived mostly at Rüschhaus near Münster, with long visits to Meersburg on Lake Constance. Born prematurely, she carried a powerful mind in a delicate, sickly frame all her life. Her gifts joined inexhaustible imagination with keen observation and a quaint, facile poetic language.

Her uncles August and Werner von Haxthausen drew her into the romantic movement, and Sprickmann first trained her in verse. Schlüter, her longtime mentor, with Junkmann, first brought her poems before the public in 1838, though unhappily chosen. Later editions by Schücking, Kreiten, and Arens, plus her edited letters, secured her standing. Her Geistliches Jahr remained unfinished at her death, its concluding part left incomplete.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-freiherr-von-:
Josef von Eichendorff, called the last champion of romanticism, was a German poet and storyteller of the early nineteenth century. Born in 1788 at the family castle of Lubowitz in Upper Silesia, he studied at Halle and Heidelberg. There he fell in with the Romantic school and its leaders Görres, Arnim, and Brentano. His first poems appeared while he was still a student.

Eichendorff left books and law in 1813 to join the Lützow volunteers against Napoleon, and he marched again in 1815, entering Paris with the victors. After 1816 he served Prussia as a civil servant, first at Danzig and later in Berlin's ministry of worship. His best-loved work remains the novella about a good-for-nothing wanderer, Aus dem Leben eines Taugenichts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-dering:
George Dering Wolff, an editor born in West Virginia in 1822, carried German Reformed learning into Catholic journalism. Son of a Reformed divine, he graduated from Marshall College, studied law, and, though admitted to the bar, took a four-year theology course and became a Reformed minister. He followed Nevin's Mercersburg school, which treated Christ's Church as a living organism and sought to restore truths the Reformation had dropped.

Seeing his tenets' inconsistency at last, Wolff joined the Catholic Church in 1871. He edited Baltimore's Catholic Mirror, then Philadelphia's Catholic Standard until his death as editor-in-chief. In 1876 he helped Corcoran and O'Connor found the American Catholic Quarterly Review. His pieces ran largely to apologetic theology. His wife and his brother also became Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-philip:
George Philipp Ludolf von Beckedorff, a Prussian official born at Hanover in 1778, rose high, converted, and was cast out. After theology at Jena and a medical degree at Göttingen in 1799, he tutored Anhalt-Bernburg's crown prince from 1810, then entered Prussia's High Privy Council and Ministry of Public Worship. As schools supervisor with Nicolovius he lifted popular education and issued a nine-volume Year Book of the Prussian Schools.

Study of the sects convinced Beckedorff that Rome was the true apostolic Church, and a beloved child's death decided him. After days with Bishop Sailer he abjured and communicated in June 1827, and dismissal followed at once. Retired to Grünhof, he built a church and school for scattered Catholics and poor children. Under Frederick William he regained honor, nobility, and the state agricultural department's presidency. His Catholic Truth, Words of Peace, ran three editions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-llandaff:
Llandaff is an ancient Welsh diocese whose roots lie in the sixth-century monastic movement led by Dubricius. His pupil Teilo became abbot of the daughter house at Llandaff, which grew into the chief monastery after Dubricius withdrew to Bardsey.

Early abbots held episcopal rank, and Teilo and Dubricius are even called archbishops, though the title then meant rule over monasteries, not a province. Welsh bishops long stood apart from Rome's missionaries, and only in 768 took the Roman Easter reckoning. After the Norman Conquest, Canterbury claimed oversight, and Llandaff became its suffragan under Bishop Urban.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mohileff:
Mohileff was the Latin Catholic archdiocese and church province for Catholics under Russian rule. This entry follows its tangled birth and troubled history. Before Poland's partition, only scattered mission stations served Russia's few Catholics. Jesuits laboured in Moscow from 1648 and built its first Catholic church in 1691.

After the partitions brought hundreds of thousands of Catholics under the tsars, Empress Catherine set up the Diocese of White Russia at Mohileff in 1772. She acted without consulting the pope, then raised it to an archdiocese a decade later. Rome eventually recognised it. Later rulers squeezed it hard, suppressing sees and leaving archdioceses vacant for years. Only the 1905 toleration edicts eased the pressure, and local officials soon whittled that easing away.
doe-osti-3015048-measuring-the-energy-co:
Energy use by deep neural networks is measured at the wall in NLR/TP-2C00-91181, dated January 2026, from the National Laboratory of the Rockies with Carnegie Mellon University. Against the Red-AI trend of ever larger training runs, the team built BUTTER-E, a dataset of 41,129 experimental runs across 30,582 network configurations, all metered at node level on CPUs and GPUs. Charles Edison Tripp led the author team.

The runs span 13 datasets, 20 network sizes, 8 shapes, and 14 depths. Analysis finds a surprise: efficiency does not fall in a straight line as parameters or FLOPs shrink, because hardware and memory hierarchy mediate the result. The authors fit a simple energy model covering size, compute, and memory traffic, and close with design recommendations favoring cache-considerate algorithms and hardware codesign.
doe-osti-3015810-gateway-cities-unplugge:
Darien Crimmin, Adarsh Ajithkumar, Christina McPike, and colleagues wrote this final technical report on a project called Gateway Cities Unplugged. The project tackled a plain problem: apartment buildings that serve low and moderate income households rarely take part in grid modernization. Yet multifamily housing uses a large share of the nation's building energy, and its owners face high costs and aging systems.

The team audited six representative multifamily properties across Massachusetts, Connecticut, and New York, then designed technology packages meant to pay their way. Packages combined supervisory controls, smart thermostats, battery storage, and solar panels. The work also produced a screening tool, the GEB Calculator, which totals costs, savings, and possible program revenue for a whole portfolio. Building owners can use the results to judge where flexible, efficient upgrades make sense first.
doe-osti-3098593-oneida-indian-nation-fa:
Bryan Mignone and Matthew Johnston report final results for the Oneida Indian Nation under award DE-IE0000124, dated April 29, 2026. Total project costs came to about 1.96 million dollars, with a federal share near 1.46 million. Guided by a 2018 energy audit, the Nation upgraded nearly 30 of its buildings. Crews installed LED lighting, high-efficiency heating and cooling gear, programmable thermostats, variable speed drives, and kitchen exhaust controls.

Work at the Turning Stone Resort and Casino campus finished first, live by December 31, 2022, with checks starting the next day. The wider rollout across 28 Nation facilities ran in phases through 2024. Some planned heating unit swaps were dropped after staff found those units already replaced under the standard 20-year refresh cycle. Savings were tracked in the B3 benchmarking tool.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MeekJeff_Meek_J: A letter dated April 28, 1979 concerns the manuscript of John Joerg, and it is filed under the name Jeff Meek. Letters about manuscripts in these files usually pass between researchers, editors, and would-be publishers of assassination work. The file gives the date and the manuscript's author. It does not name the letter's writer or say what stage the manuscript had reached, so its contents cannot be described further.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_colombia:
Inside Chiquita's Colombia operation, staff on the ground were uneasy about money the company paid to armed groups. Michael Evans edited this briefing book, posted in May 2017, from the company's own papers. Top executives, the records show, grew comfortable with the payments even as questions rose.

Staff in Colombia asked whether Chiquita had gone past paying extortion. They feared the company was directly funding leftist guerrillas and right-wing paramilitary groups alike. That split between worried local staff and calm headquarters is the heart of the record, and it shows how a payment scheme looks from inside the firm that ran it.
michael-strogoff:
Jules Verne published Michael Strogoff in 1876, as part of his Extraordinary Voyages series. The novel opens at a brilliant fete in the New Palace at St. Petersburg. Word arrives that the telegraph wire is cut beyond Tomsk. A Tatar rebellion led by the Khan Feofar is rising in Siberia.

The Czar chooses his courier Michael Strogoff for a desperate mission. Strogoff must cross rebellious Siberia to reach besieged Irkutsk. There he must warn the Czar's brother about a traitor. The publisher's note calls it one of Verne's best books, and its ride across Russia made it famous.
mike-flannery-on-duty-and-off:
Ellis Parker Butler published this story collection with Doubleday, Page and Company in 1909. Its hero is Mike Flannery, the express agent at Westcote. The book holds three long tales: Just Like a Cat, The Three Hundred, and Fleas Will Be Fleas. Gustavus C. Widney supplied the illustrations.

In the opening story, Flannery watches workmen tear the top off Seiler's Hill behind his office. Their wagons dump clay into a swamp that will soon become streets and houses. Flannery hopes the growth will finally earn him real help. Butler tells his tales in Flannery's Irish-American voice, mixing small-town business with broad comedy.
nasa-tm-19710020807-flight-investigation:
Nick E. Samanich and Roger Chamberlin of the Lewis Research Center wrote this flight study, NASA TM X-2295, on a plug nozzle mounted beneath a wing. Several nozzle configurations were installed on an underwing nacelle of an F-106B aircraft. A J85 turbojet engine supplied the exhaust flow for the tests.

The team compared installed performance with isolated cold-flow results from a scale model in a Lewis wind tunnel. They varied plug truncation, shroud extension, secondary cooling flow, and nozzle pressure ratio, and also changed the nacelle shape ahead of the nozzle. The summary reports that installation had little effect near the top of the subsonic range. It hurt at lower speeds and just above Mach one. Installed performance actually peaked higher than the isolated data, thanks to pressure effects from the wing and nacelle flow fields.
one-third-off:
Irvin Shrewsbury Cobb wrote this book of wit and humor. George Doran published his works in New York. The frontispiece shows Cobb weighing himself with shock. Its caption jokes that he credited himself a profound shock. The title promises a plea from a man reducing.

Cobb lists earlier books of fiction, humor, and miscellany. Titles include Old Judge Priest and Cobb's Anatomy. Eating in several languages is one comic theme here. The abandoned farmers and the life of the party follow. Cobb was a famed American humorist and journalist. His self-mockery made dieting a source of laughter.
polly-of-the-hospital-staff:
Emma C. Dowd published Polly of the Hospital Staff in Boston with Houghton Mifflin in 1912, dedicating it to the mother of Polly. Her heroine is a small, lame girl whose cherry-pudding story opens the book and whose election by the children's ward follows: the patients themselves choose Polly as their sunbeam. Contents move through birthdays, a little sad lady, a night of song, and Polly playing Eva in a ward performance.

Trouble comes with a kidnapping and a bid for Polly, since a lovable child in a hospital is a child several households want. The illustrations list ends with a document that makes her legally a daughter, and the contents end with a wedding, the staff's own. Dowd wrote sunshine literature with a purpose: to show cheerfulness as a form of care. Polly's success made her the first of a line of glad girls in American children's books.
song-of-roland-scott-moncrieff:
The Song of Roland, France's oldest great epic, was composed around 1140 and survives in the Oxford manuscript. C. K. Scott Moncrieff's English translation renders its ringing verse. The poem sings of Charlemagne's Spanish campaign of 778 and the ambush at Roncesvalles.

Roland, the emperor's nephew, leads the rear guard through the Pyrenees pass. Betrayed by Ganelon, he faces a vast Saracen host and refuses, from pride, to blow his horn for help until too late. His death, sword Durendal in hand, is the poem's summit. Charlemagne's vengeance and Ganelon's trial close the song. It founded the whole line of French chansons de geste.
the-love-tiff:
The Love-Tiff is an English version of Molière's Le Dépit amoureux, a comedy in five acts first represented at Béziers toward the end of 1656. An introductory notice explains that the play joins two pieces. The longer part modestly imitates a coarse Italian comedy, L'Interesse by Nicolo Secchi, and turns on a girl substituted for a boy, a device Shakespeare also used.

The notice praises the parts that are Molière's alone, including the quarrel between Éraste and Lucile that gives the play its title, and their reconciliation. It also puzzles over earlier translators who renamed the servant Gros-René, one calling him punch-gutted Ben and another Hugh. Plot, the notice admits, is over-complicated and the ending unnatural, yet the characters move through errors with no visible way out.
views-a-foot-or-europe-seen-with-knapsac:
J. Bayard Taylor wrote Views A-Foot, or Europe Seen with Knapsack and Staff, a young man's walk across Europe in two parts. Copyright was entered in 1846 by Wiley and Putnam at New York. N. P. Willis, who wrote the preface, says the book needs little introduction, since it tells its own story well. His interest, he admits, is that of an early fan of Taylor's talent.

Willis recalls that Taylor's poems, written while he was still a printer's apprentice, struck him hard, and that he praised them in the newspaper he then edited. Letters followed, and then friendship. The motto from The Winter's Tale urges the walker to jog on and keep a merry heart, since a merry heart goes all the day. Readers get the record of a poor, keen American seeing the old world on foot, with a famous editor's blessing at the door.
